Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

vignette:
Since the stalking began, Lien, a 48-year-old Vietnamese American waitress, has described her life as having split into a before and an after. She had been living alone after her divorce, working long shifts in a neighborhood restaurant where the rhythm of familiar customers and the close choreography of the dining room once gave her a sense of purpose. The stalking developed over weeks: repeated appearances outside her apartment building, the sense of being watched on her walk to work, and the shock of recognizing the same presence again near the restaurant at closing time. What remains with her is not a story she can tell in a clear sequence. When she tries, her words falter and she goes quiet, saying it is as if the worst parts do not come back as sentences but as a bodily certainty that something terrible is about to happen. At times the memory forces itself into her mind without warning, and at other moments it feels strangely unreal, almost as though it happened to another woman and not to her.

In the months that followed, Lien came to believe that whatever had once made her lively was gone for good. She says she used to be a happy person, someone who laughed easily with coworkers and chatted with regulars, but now she feels miserable almost all the time. More troubling to her is the deadened quality of her inner life: she tells the therapist that she feels dead inside, and that nothing in her days seems meaningful anymore beyond getting through a shift and getting the locks checked at night. From that bleak view of herself and her life, she has increasingly pulled away from people she used to know, ignoring invitations from former friends and avoiding social contact because being with them only reminds her of the person she was before. The same sense of inner emptiness has made her avoid anything that might bring her into herself physically; even noticing her own body feels intolerable, as if paying attention to it would force her too close to feelings she cannot bear.

Those beliefs have also sharpened the sense that danger is everywhere. Because she feels permanently changed and no longer able to trust her own safety, unfamiliar places seem especially threatening; if she cannot immediately map an exit or judge who is around her, she would rather not go at all. At home she listens constantly for small noises that might mean someone is entering. A creak in the hallway or a sound near the door can bring on a rush of physical alarm so strong that her heart pounds and her body reacts before she has fully understood what she heard. Each episode leaves her more certain that her world has narrowed into something joyless and unsafe.

The memory itself feeds this. Because it comes uninvited and cannot be put fully into words, Lien has started arranging her life around not setting it off. At the restaurant, if customers begin arguing at a table or a coworker raises their voice in the kitchen, she finds a reason to move away, unable to tolerate any hint of confrontation. She no longer stays after shifts to talk with staff she once socialized with, because familiar faces can unexpectedly pull the memory into the room with her. When the memory intrudes, it often arrives with no narrative, just fragments and a dislocated feeling that this cannot really be hers, and in those moments she scans even more intensely for danger, listening for footsteps outside her apartment door or searching a room for signs that someone could be watching her.

That vigilance has gradually shaped her behavior further. At work, she asks for predictable sections and avoids errands that would take her somewhere new. She hurries straight home after closing rather than stopping at the market or visiting anyone. Any situation that might involve disagreement feels too risky, because conflict seems like the kind of moment in which she could become trapped or exposed. The more she organizes her days around preventing danger, the less life contains anything beyond prevention itself, and this has deepened her conviction that happiness and meaning are no longer available to her.

Avoidance has not brought relief. If anything, all the effort not to think, not to feel, not to be near reminders seems to leave the memory less settled and more intrusive, returning abruptly when she is folding laundry or setting down plates at work. Each new intrusion confirms for her that she is not herself anymore, that she is empty where she used to feel alive. By the time she sought help, what frightened Lien most was not only that the fear had never really stopped, but that her life had become organized around it so completely that she could no longer imagine how to get back to being a person who felt present, safe, or real.
